analysis.one_liner: Ends the federal shield that blocks shooting victims from suing gun makers and dealers.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced and died there when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal law currently bars most lawsuits against gun and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, and dealers for harms caused when someone criminally misuses a firearm — a protection no other consumer product industry has. This bill would repeal that law, so victims of shootings and their families could sue in state or federal court like they can with any other product. The bill was introduced by Sen. Richard Blumenthal with 14 cosponsors and never moved past committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Shooting victims and their families, who under current law generally cannot sue gun sellers or manufacturers even when a sale was negligent, and who could seek damages in court if the shield were repealed. Local governments that have tried to recover shooting-related costs could also bring claims.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the core provisions of the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act, which prohibit civil suits and administrative proceedings against firearm or ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, dealers, and trade associations over criminal or unlawful misuse of a gun.

Once repealed, victims could bring civil actions in state or federal court against the gun industry for harms caused by unlawful use of a firearm, putting guns under the same liability rules that apply to cars, drugs, and other consumer products.

analysis.who_pays: The firearms industry — manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations — would face lawsuits, legal defense costs, potential damage awards, and higher liability insurance. Some of those costs could be passed to lawful gun buyers through higher prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and trade groups

drawbacks.text: The repeal would allow suits over criminal misuse by third parties, and the industry's core argument for the shield is that sellers cannot control what a criminal does with a lawfully sold product; without the shield, even small dealers could face expensive litigation over sales they did not foresee being misused.
The prospect of large judgments could drive some small dealers out of business or be recovered through higher gun prices, costs borne partly by law-abiding buyers.
Repeal does not guarantee wins for plaintiffs — it only restores the right to sue — so many cases could still fail on the merits after years and significant expense.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The central question is whether one industry deserves blanket immunity from negligence suits that no other manufacturer enjoys. Restoring the right to sue gives victims a real remedy and creates a financial incentive for safer sales practices; the honest cost is a heavier litigation burden on gun sellers, especially small dealers, and no guarantee that any individual lawsuit succeeds. The scale of harm at stake — deaths and injuries from foreseeable criminal misuse — is large, but the bill offered no middle-ground limits on which suits could proceed.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the day it was introduced, never received a hearing or vote, and expired when the 114th Congress ended in January 2017.

narrative.text: Sen. Richard Blumenthal introduced the bill on January 27, 2016, joined by eight Democratic senators as original cosponsors.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day; that was the last action the bill ever received.
The bill carried 14 total cosponsors — 13 Democrats and 1 Independent — and never reached the Senate floor before the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.
Under Senate rules, a bill that is not approved by its committee or brought to the floor dies at the end of the two-year Congress and must start over from scratch in the next one.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Gun manufacturers, dealers, and their trade associations, which keep the federal law that blocks most negligence lawsuits against them. Shooting victims and their families remain unable to sue, and the status quo the bill targeted is unchanged.

for.name: Sen. Richard Blumenthal
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the gun industry's lawsuit shield and gathered cosponsors.

for.name: Original cosponsors: Sens. Chris Murphy, Ed Markey, Dick Durbin, Dianne Feinstein, Tim Kaine, Patty Murray, Ron Wyden, and Kirsten Gillibrand
for.role: Democratic senators who signed on at introduction
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, bringing it to 14 total cosponsors.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: The committee he chaired received the bill by referral and never scheduled a hearing or vote on it in the year the Congress had left.

against.name: National Rifle Association and firearms industry groups
against.role: Industry advocates for the lawsuit shield
against.what_they_did: Defended the Protection of Lawful Commerce in Arms Act as essential protection for lawful gun sellers and opposed efforts to repeal it.

sides.party_line_note: Every sponsor and cosponsor was a Democrat or Independent; no Republican signed on, and the Republican-controlled Judiciary Committee took no action on the bill.

industries.industry: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers, sellers, importers, and dealers
industries.note: The bill would strip the federal immunity that blocks most negligence suits against the gun trade over criminal misuse of its products — a liability shield no other consumer industry has. The industry kept that shield, so victims of shootings continue to bear their own medical, funeral, and lost-income costs with no court remedy.

The law the bill repeals explicitly protects industry trade groups from suit as well, so repeal would have exposed them to litigation too. Their protection survives because the bill died in committee.
